The echo still arrived while green was held: it briefly shifted north by about 0.1 brick, then returned to the held position (turn 42). Holding constrains the response rather than preventing the event.
Green remained still after release (turn 43). To distinguish velocity replacement from addition without floor-spin effects, I will arrange an echo while green is airborne.

The echo is due in 0.88 counts (turn 45). A northward throw at 60 degrees with impulse 6 should keep green airborne across that time.

Turn 47 resolves the ambiguity: at the echo, airborne green’s northward motion stopped at y=0.8, eastward motion began, and its fall slowed as if vertical speed reset to zero. Green’s y remained 0.8 through landing and rest (turn 48), confirming airborne velocity replacement. I will now test whether the stored velocity is red’s total post-command velocity or just the commanded increment.

Best-supported rule: each red PUSH/THROW schedules its total post-command translational velocity to overwrite green’s 12 counts later.

Main discovery: red PUSH/THROW commands cause a one-way delayed velocity transfer to green, approximately 12 counts later. Onset timing matched exactly to the recorded resolution (turns 15–17); vertical throws also transferred (18–21). Green and blue commands produced no corresponding response in the other balls over 14.12-count control windows (22–25). This is not continuous path copying: stopping red by grasping did not stop green’s later full motion (29–31), and moving, releasing, and dropping red produced no echo (32–34). Airborne tests show that the delayed event replaces green’s translational velocity: its prior northward motion ceased and its vertical descent reset when an eastward echo arrived (44–48). Two closely spaced commands support recording red’s total post-command velocity, not just the latest increment (49–52). Holding green allowed a brief displacement at the scheduled time, followed by return to its held position (40–43). Ordinary motion: equal impulse-4 floor pushes moved all three about 5.8 bricks; red’s impulse-2 push moved about 1.5 bricks, consistent with roughly quadratic stopping-distance scaling. A vertical impulse-4 throw rose about 0.8 bricks above resting height. Limitations: positions are rounded, some trajectories are compressed, counts have no supplied conversion to seconds, and angular velocity was not measured. Residual spin may explain floor drift after velocity replacement; the apparent northern boundary near y=5.9 was not independently tested.
